entities.summary:
Anaxagoras (c. 500 – 427 BCE), a seminal Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher, introduced a radical new cosmology and a sophisticated materialist philosophy to Athens, profoundly influencing key figures like Pericles, Euripides, and Socrates. Hailing from Clazomenae in Ionia, a region then under the sway of the Persian Empire, he brought with him a sophisticated understanding of the natural world that challenged traditional mythological explanations prevalent in the burgeoning Athenian democracy. His arrival marked a pivotal moment in the intellectual development of the Classical Age, shifting philosophical focus from purely cosmic origins to the material composition of reality and the role of an ordering intelligence.

Anaxagoras posited a universe composed of an infinite number of infinitesimal "seeds" or "homoeomeries," each containing portions of all qualities, which were ordered by an external, intelligent force he termed *Nous* (Mind). He famously asserted that the sun was a red-hot stone larger than the Peloponnese and the moon was an earthy body reflecting sunlight, suggesting that celestial bodies were not divine but physical objects. This materialistic interpretation extended to eclipses, which he correctly explained as shadows cast by the earth or moon, and even to the nature of sensation and thought, which he attributed to physical processes, laying groundwork for later scientific inquiry.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Anaxagoras played a pivotal role in shifting Greek philosophical inquiry from mythological to rational explanations for the cosmos, significantly influencing Athenian intellectual life and later thinkers like Plato and Aristotle. His trial for impiety also set a critical precedent for the persecution of philosophical dissent within the Athenian legal system.
